title: Pathophysiology: Innate & Adaptive Immunity—Defense, Memory and Dysregulation
html:
The immune system protects the body by recognizing danger, limiting invasion, removing damaged cells, and remembering selected antigens. Effective defense also requires tolerance: the ability to avoid attacking normal self-tissue. Too little immune activity raises infection risk; excessive or misdirected activity can produce allergy, autoimmunity, inflammation, and organ injury.

Learning goals

  • Compare barrier, innate, and adaptive defenses.
  • Explain how phagocytes, natural killer cells, complement, B cells, and T cells contribute to protection.
  • Connect antigen presentation with activation of adaptive immunity.
  • Distinguish active from passive immunity and primary from secondary immune responses.
  • Recognize the four hypersensitivity patterns, loss of self-tolerance, and immune deficiency.
  • Prioritize anaphylaxis and serious infection in an immunocompromised client.

Defense begins at barriers

Intact skin, mucous membranes, cilia, tears, saliva, gastric acidity, urine flow, and resident microorganisms reduce entry and colonization. These defenses are present before a specific antigen is recognized. Burns, wounds, invasive devices, impaired cough, poor perfusion, and disruption of the microbiome can weaken them.

Assess the host, not only the organism
Age, nutrition, vaccination history, chronic disease, surgery, devices, medications, leukocyte function, and prior exposures influence whether exposure becomes disease and whether classic inflammatory findings appear.

Innate immunity is rapid and broadly targeted

Innate immunity responds within minutes to recurring molecular patterns associated with microbes or tissue damage. It does not require a previous encounter with the exact antigen. Neutrophils and macrophages engulf and destroy targets; dendritic cells capture antigen and help activate adaptive immunity; natural killer cells can kill stressed or infected cells without the antigen-specific receptor rearrangement used by lymphocytes.

Inflammatory mediators recruit leukocytes and change local blood flow and permeability. This rapid response can contain a threat, but excessive activation can damage tissue and contribute to systemic instability. An immunocompromised client may have serious infection with little redness, pus, fever, or leukocytosis.

Complement amplifies defense

The classical, lectin, and alternative pathways activate through different triggers but converge on a shared cascade. Complement fragments can coat a target to improve phagocytosis (opsonization), attract and activate inflammatory cells, and form a membrane attack complex that damages susceptible organisms. Regulatory proteins normally protect host cells; unregulated activation can injure tissue.

Antigen presentation connects innate and adaptive immunity

Dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells process antigens and display fragments with major histocompatibility complex molecules. They travel to lymphoid tissue and provide antigen plus costimulatory signals to lymphocytes. This bridge allows a rapid innate alarm to generate a highly specific adaptive response.

Adaptive immunity is specific and creates memory

Adaptive immunity develops more slowly during a first encounter because rare antigen-specific lymphocytes must be activated and expanded. B lymphocytes can become plasma cells that secrete antibodies and memory B cells that support future responses. CD4 helper T cells coordinate immune activity through cell contact and cytokines. CD8 cytotoxic T cells destroy selected infected or abnormal cells. Memory B and T cells respond more rapidly and effectively when the antigen returns.

Antibodies have specialized roles

  • IgM is commonly the first antibody produced in a primary response and efficiently activates complement.
  • IgG is the major serum antibody in many secondary responses, supports neutralization and opsonization, and crosses the placenta.
  • IgA protects mucosal surfaces and is present in secretions, including breast milk.
  • IgE binds mast cells and participates in immediate allergy and defense against some parasites.
  • IgD primarily functions as a receptor on naïve B cells.

An antibody class can suggest a mechanism, but no single immunoglobulin value diagnoses a complete clinical condition. Interpret results with timing, symptoms, exposure, immune status, and the specific assay.

Active and passive immunity are different

Active immunity develops when a person's immune system responds to an antigen through infection or vaccination. It takes time to develop and can create durable memory. Passive immunity transfers preformed antibodies, such as maternal IgG across the placenta or prescribed immune globulin. It can provide immediate protection but is temporary and does not create the recipient's own durable immune memory.

Vaccination recommendations depend on age, health status, prior doses, exposure, pregnancy, and immune function. Some live vaccines may be unsafe or ineffective in certain immunocompromised clients. The RN screens for contraindications and precautions and follows current guidance and orders rather than making assumptions from the vaccine name alone.

Primary and secondary responses explain immune memory

During a primary exposure, recognition, clonal expansion, and antibody production take time. Re-exposure activates memory cells, usually producing a faster and stronger response. This is the basis for vaccination and booster strategies. A measurable antibody is only one part of protection; cell-mediated immunity and timing also matter.

Hypersensitivity is an injurious immune response

  • Type I: immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell activation. Findings may include urticaria, bronchospasm, angioedema, vomiting, and anaphylaxis.
  • Type II: antibodies target antigens on cells or tissues, producing cell injury or altered receptor function.
  • Type III: antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissue and activate complement and inflammation.
  • Type IV: delayed T-cell-mediated injury rather than antibody-mediated injury.

The categories describe mechanisms; the priority is the client's current stability. After a likely allergen exposure, wheezing, stridor, hypotension, rapidly progressing swelling, or collapse requires immediate emergency response even if a rash is absent.

Anaphylaxis is an airway and circulation emergency

Stop the suspected trigger when feasible, call for emergency assistance, assess airway, breathing, circulation, and perfusion, and administer intramuscular epinephrine promptly according to protocol or order. Position, oxygen, fluids, additional medications, and monitoring follow the clinical situation and protocol. Antihistamines do not replace epinephrine for airway compromise or shock. Continue reassessment because symptoms can recur after initial improvement.

Autoimmunity reflects loss of self-tolerance

Central and peripheral tolerance normally remove, silence, or regulate self-reactive lymphocytes. Genetic susceptibility, environmental triggers, infection, hormones, and failures of regulation can contribute to autoimmune disease. Tissue injury may be antibody-mediated, immune-complex-mediated, T-cell-mediated, or a combination. Manifestations depend on the affected organs, and immunosuppressive treatment can trade inflammatory control for greater infection risk.

Immune deficiency may be primary or acquired

Primary immunodeficiencies arise from inherited defects. Secondary immune impairment is more common and can result from malnutrition, malignancy, human immunodeficiency virus, diabetes, organ failure, loss of splenic function, corticosteroids, chemotherapy, transplantation therapy, or other causes. The infection pattern offers clues: recurrent, severe, persistent, unusual, or opportunistic infections warrant evaluation.

A complete blood count with differential and absolute neutrophil count help assess cellular risk, while immunoglobulin levels, complement tests, lymphocyte studies, cultures, and targeted serology answer different questions. A normal total white blood cell count does not prove normal immune function.

Neutropenic fever is time-sensitive
A new fever in a client with severe neutropenia may be the only early sign of a life-threatening infection. Follow the organization's urgent pathway, obtain prescribed cultures without delaying time-critical antimicrobial therapy, and protect the client from additional exposure.

Translate immunity into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize: Identify exposure, onset, airway or perfusion change, infection pattern, medications, devices, vaccination history, and immune risk.
  2. Analyze: Link the cue cluster to barrier failure, innate or adaptive dysfunction, allergy, autoimmunity, treatment effect, or infection.
  3. Prioritize: Anaphylaxis, shock, respiratory distress, altered mental status, and possible infection during severe neutropenia outrank routine teaching.
  4. Generate: Plan protection, escalation, ordered specimens and treatment, symptom support, and client education.
  5. Act: Use emergency protocols when indicated, protect asepsis, administer prescribed therapy, and communicate the complete risk pattern.
  6. Evaluate: Trend airway, perfusion, temperature, symptoms, laboratory findings, treatment response, adverse effects, and recurrence.

Clinical example

A client receiving chemotherapy reports chills and fatigue. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), but the IV site has no redness and the total white blood cell count is not elevated. The absolute neutrophil count is severely reduced. The lack of local inflammation does not reassure the RN. The client has a time-sensitive infection risk, so the RN assesses stability, activates the neutropenic-fever pathway, obtains ordered specimens, supports timely treatment, and reassesses for organ dysfunction.
